# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–40 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final Revision 18)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Autumn of tenth year after Waterloo (1831), extending into winter. Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner (Chapters 1–35) through Chapter 36 (winter into summer) to Chapters 37–38 (spring/early summer) to Chapter 39 (autumn, village scenes) to **Chapter 40 (winter; Imperial dinner preparations, elopement aftermath, harbor town scenes, forgery rumors in City).**
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Bruton Street, Queen's Gate, Islington, City Road Music-Hall, Cannon Street Hotel, Euston Square, Liverpool, Conservative club in the City, Mount Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Southend; Harrowgate; Lowestoft; Dunholt; Staveton; Gulton; Dunwick; Salford; Yarlton; Salwick; Beccles (Suffolk); coastal towns; rural areas (Sheep's Acre Farm, Salmere, Mirecombe, Miremere); harbor towns (Staveton, Salwick).

## Major Deaths
John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt, Wevie Lindner (died winter, buried Salmere). Conar Hollett (drowned crossing estuary at Gulton; no body seen; Halan Hollett reported it at inn). Feten Lindner followed her to Harrowgate within the month (likely died).

## Rebecca's Arc
Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives allowance but refuses to see her. Appears wealthy at Bath/Cheltenham, busies herself with piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
Married at Ostend; Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; daughter Jane his pride.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Welbeck Street resident. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review; praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" (Mr. Broune). Rejected Mr. Broune's proposal via letter; full of regrets; in debt. Overdrawing her account at bank. Chapter 39: Discovered Felix's failed elopement plan; helped him to bed early morning Wednesday after he arrived drunk. Suffering over his involvement with Marie Melmotte's elopement, money owed. Confessed troubles to Mr. Broune (Thursday evening). Received his counsel: must rid herself of Felix, extract money story, send word to him early next morning. Sent letter to Mr. Broune with Felix's account: claims Melmotte owed him £600; received £250 from Marie via Didon; lost this money at play. Acknowledged in letter she cannot justify believing her son's account.

**Felix Carbury**: Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Won substantial sums at gaming. **Chapter 38–39 (ELOPEMENT PLAN FAILED)**: Received £250 from Didon Monday 4 P.M.; understood he must go to New York. Planned passage Tuesday under name "Walter Jones"; attempted to meet Ruby at Music Hall but she did not appear. Returned to club, found Dolly Longestaffe and Miles Grendall; whispered to Grendall to convert I.O.U.s to cash; Grendall refused. Had been drinking freely; called Grendall to card-room with Dolly as witness; Grendall again refused. Played at Beargarden till 4 A.M.; intoxicated and almost penniless; made unpleasant remarks about Miles Grendall; desperate row ensued. **Between 6–7 A.M. Wednesday knocked at Welbeck Street door; lady Carbury opened door; he was sodden with gutter, drunk. Lied claiming "old shap stopped ush" (Melmotte); Melmotte was actually asleep in Grosvenor Square, ignorant of plot. Felix stumbled upstairs; mother removed his clothes and boots; he fell asleep. Still in bed Thursday, 2–5 P.M., sick and ill and sore from head to foot. Remained in bed Friday morning awaiting refreshment. Still in London as of Chapter 40.** **Chapter 40: Marie realizes Sir Felix has not come for her; questions his pluck and truthfulness; wonders why he does not tell her truth; fears reason for his absence would be prejudicial to her love.**

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit (too young, age disparity). Paul returned "as still dear friend" within week, promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. Roger declared love anew; determination unshaken. Paul thoroughly in love with her. Chapter 36: Paul visited her at Welbeck Street; she told mother loves someone else and praises Roger. **Chapter 39: Retired from sofa while mother attended Felix. Turned matter over in mind: Could it be right to marry one man when loves another?** Did not know how to give herself into arms of man she did not love.

## Marie Melmotte and Elopement Attempt

**Marie Melmotte**: **Chapter 38 (ELOPEMENT EXECUTED BUT INTERCEPTED)**: Sat up all night packing treasures with Didon; discussed American clergyman marrying them on board. **6 A.M. Wednesday: Robert departed first with big boxes. Marie and Didon followed in second cab with smaller luggage. Reached Euston Square, obtained tickets in French, departed. ELOPEMENT INTERCEPTED AT LIVERPOOL PLATFORM: Gentleman addressed her: "You, I think, are Miss Melmotte." Didon became voluble in French. Gentleman insisted, used her English. Marie declared she spoke French; he countered she spoke English too. Gentleman told them to return to London; would accompany them. Gentleman telegraphed Grosvenor Square during journey. At Euston Square met by Melmotte carriage. Marie taken home; boxes to follow.** **Chapter 39: Marie aware she would be interrogated. Melmotte held her very hard, shook her while speaking, reminding her of generosity. Marie shows determination: "I don't think that mamma cares. It's papa. I'd do it again to-morrow if I had the chance." She continued: "I would. Why is a girl to be made to marry to please any one but herself? I won't. And it's very mean saying that I stole the money. I always take what I want, and papa never says anything about it." Melmotte angry at Sir Felix beyond measure; man pledged in writing to abstain from marrying Marie. Learned all details of cheque for £250. Melmotte would prosecute baronet if possible. Received £250 back from Mr. Broune. Decided to write to Lord Nidderdale, making clear breast of matter; believes openness best supports chance of keeping young lord to his suit. Urged Nidderdale to renew suit; emphasized Marie never gave Nidderdale encouragement since Christmas.** **Chapter 40: Monday lunch at Bruton Street house. Nidderdale got up and shook hands with Marie; she put brave face upon it, struggled hard in midst of very real difficulties, succeeded in saying ordinary word or two. Her position uncomfortable. Girl who ran away without her lover and was brought back found state of mind peculiarly harassing. Marie's courage good; she ate her lunch next to Lord Nidderdale. Later, Lord Nidderdale renewed suit in drawing-room at Grosvenor Square. Marie passionately rejected him, declaring: "If we had cared for each other they couldn't have broken it off... You never cared for me a bit more than for the old woman at the crossing... You'd better go away." Broke down sobbing, confessed loves Sir Felix Carbury more than any person in world; refused Nidderdale's advances. Upon leaving, Nidderdale reflected he had "prospered, considering the extreme difficulties," thought her "quite a different sort of girl" and "awfully jolly." Marie afterward walked about room almost in dismay, realizing Sir Felix not entirely as nice as thought him. Acknowledged his beauty but could trust him for no other good quality. Questions why he does not come, why he does not show pluck, why he does not tell truth. Believed Lord Nidderdale's hint that he knows cause keeping Felix from Liverpool; believed cause must be prejudicial to her love. Thought if Nidderdale had courted her initially as he just attempted, she would have submitted herself to be cut in pieces for him.**

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Crisis, Correspondence, and Resolution (Chapter 39)**: Returned to London Monday from Suffolk. Sat in lodgings thinking of his condition. Promised to go to Islington; aware if he failed she would come to him. **Wrote to Mrs. Hurtle: acknowledged circumstances made their lives and temperaments too different for happy marriage; fault was his; better to own fault and take consequences than marry with consciousness marriage would be sorrow and repentance. Broke engagement before knowing this girl; did not break because came to love her. No grounds for hoping love will lead to results. Told her condition of mind exactly. If possible would compensate injury or undergo retribution; could she exact? Thought further meeting avail nothing. But if she wishes, will come last time.** **Mrs. Hurtle's Response**: Letter duly reached Paul. She suffered many injuries; this worst, most unpardonable, most unmanly. Called him coward, false liar. He bound himself by most solemn obligation, then told her they go for nothing because do not suit his view. Called him coward. Talked of compensation; does he mean money? As to retribution: yes. He shall suffer. Desires him to come to her with horsewhip in hand. Will whip him till has not breath in body. Should he be afraid and break promise, she will come to him; will make London too hot to hold him. **Paul started immediately for Islington upon receiving letter. Chapter 39 Meeting Details**: Paul shown into Mrs. Hurtle's room. His mind altogether intent on his own troubles. Mrs. Hurtle very calm but quietness assumed; could convert into violence at any moment; her eye foretold spring of wild-cat. Paul sat. Mrs. Hurtle spoke softly, then raised voice: "Why should a gentleman trouble himself to say any more,--than that he has changed his mind?... But I should not. I at still will be true. I should take you, Paul,--still take you; with a confidence that I should yet win you to me by my devotion. I have still some kindness of feeling towards you,--none to that woman who is I suppose younger than I, and gentler, and a maid." Asked advice what to do next. Has given up every friend for him. Has no home; Mrs. Pipkin's room more her home than any other spot. Asked: "You are in some degree responsible,--are you not,--for my loneliness?" **Paul suggested she better remain here; does good to Mrs. Pipkin. Mrs. Pipkin went into hysterics yesterday when Mrs. Hurtle spoke of leaving. Then paused, absolute silence for minute. Admitted had much more to say; handed him sheet containing threat of horsewhip. Then handed him scrap written at Lowestoft—softer letter. She said: "Nay, I would not hurt you,--not at this moment. Why should I be such a victim? There, you have seen them all. Which will you have?" Paul knelt. She said: "But it will be when you have left me. Why should you kneel there? You do not love me." She put hand upon his forehead, pushed back his hair, looked into his face. Asked: "I wonder whether that other woman loves you. I suppose you had better go." Took his hand and pressed it to her breast. Asked: "Tell me one thing. When you spoke of--compensation, did you mean--money?" **After Paul left, Mrs. Hurtle announced standing upright in middle of room with smile on face: "Everything is over between me and Mr. Montague." She has decided to depart from Islington.**

## Augustus Melmotte and Imperial Reception Crisis (Chapter 39–40)

**Events Chapter 39**: Fast asleep in Grosvenor Square Wednesday morning, ignorant of elopement plot. Later interrogated Marie about cheque; held her very hard, shook her. By two o'clock matter known to everybody. Would hear of it, all trouble taken in Lord Nidderdale direction taken in vain. His anger against Sir Felix infinitely more bitter than against his daughter. Received £250 back from Mr. Broune. Invited Lord Nidderdale to lunch at Conservative club in the City before Railway Board meeting. Urged Nidderdale to visit Grosvenor Square Sunday morning about noon to renew suit with Marie. 

**Imperial Reception Confrontation (Chapter 39)**: Melmotte stood directly in way of Mr. Wilson, Secretary of State, repeated demand: "I am desirous of being presented to his Imperial Majesty. Will you do me the honour of making my request known to Mr. Wilson?" Insisting: "It is generally understood, I believe, that the Emperor is to do me the honour of dining at my poor house on Monday. He don't dine there unless I'm made acquainted with him before he comes." Lord Alfred whispered: "upon my word it isn't the thing. They're only Indian chaps and Eastern swells who are presented here." Melmotte responded: "Then they should have done it at Windsor, or at the ball. By George, Alfred! I'm in earnest, and somebody had better look to it. If I'm not presented to his Imperial Majesty to-night, by G----, there shall be no dinner in Grosvenor Square on Monday. I'm master enough of my own house." Threatened: "There shall be no dinner. I'll be d---- if any of the lot shall dine in Grosvenor Square on Monday." Under secretary Lord De Griffin intervened: "If you will be so kind as to follow me." Melmotte resolved upon making a little speech but quelled by celestial solemnity; shuffled by without saying a word. **Had gained his point. As he was taken home, was intolerable. Lord Alfred tried to escape but Melmotte insisted on his presence. Continued ranting in carriage: "D---- the election, sir. I stand before the electors of Westminster as a man of business, not as a courtier... I think myself quite as great a man as any Prince... I'll teach them a lesson before long." This went on through whole of long cigar. Afterwards, Lord Alfred slowly paced his way back to Mount Street, thinking deeply whether there might not be means of escaping from his present servitude.**

**Imperial Dinner Preparations (Chapter 39–40)**: Servants and workmen giving admittance; wreaths of flowers and green boughs being suspended, last daubs of heavy gilding given, incense being burned, tables being fixed and chairs moved; enormous set of open presses being nailed together. Hall was chaos. **Father Barham made his way to banqueting hall. Melmotte stood in front of chair arranged for Emperor, very angry indeed. Had been given to understand he was to sit opposite to august guest—immediately in face of Emperor. Now explained to him this could not be done. In face of the Emperor there must be wide space. Royal princesses who sat next to Emperor, and royal princes who sat next to princesses, must also be so indulged. Melmotte's own seat became really quite obscure. Lord Alfred having very bad time of it. Melmotte succeeded in having removed the bar which had been specially put up to prevent his intrusion on his own guests in his own house.**

**Father Barham's Visit (Chapter 40)**: Father Barham walked up the room and came close to scene of action, unperceived by either of the Grendalls. Melmotte was trying in vain to move his own seat nearer to Imperial Majesty. "Who the d---- are you?" Melmotte asked. Father Barham stood humbly with his hat off. "I am the Rev. Mr. Barham," said visitor. "I am the priest of Beccles in Suffolk. I believe I am speaking to Mr. Melmotte." Melmotte asked: "And what may you want? I don't know whether you are aware that you have found your way into my private dining-room without any introduction. Where the mischief are the fellows, Alfred, who ought to have seen about this?" **Father Barham went away disgusted; yet not altogether disheartened. Man had not declared he was not Roman Catholic. Had shown himself brute. Had blasphemed and cursed. Had been outrageously uncivil to minister of God. Had manifested himself as being no gentleman. But not the less might he be good Catholic—good enough at any rate to be influential on right side. To Father Barham's eyes, Melmotte with all his insolent vulgarity infinitely more hopeful man than Roger Carbury. Father Barham made himself believe before he returned to Beccles that Mr. Melmotte was certainly Roman Catholic.**

**Melmotte's Charitable Maneuvering**: Presented hundred guineas towards erection of altar for new church of St. Fabricius. Donation accompanied by letter leaving little doubt that new member for Westminster would be member of Catholic party in House. Mr. Alf's newspaper bit at this, noting apparent hypocrisy with Protestant support. Melmotte and his manager not foolish enough to allow it to actuate them. **Possessed only by belief that England's glory demanded his return for Westminster; thoroughly ignorant of political questions, political history, Parliament's working, nationality, or forms of government; had never read a book in his life; knew nothing of Hampden, Somers, or Pitt; yet fully confident England demanded Melmotte for Westminster. Perhaps most remarkable circumstance in career of this remarkable man was fact that he came almost to believe in himself.**

**Chapter 40 - Melmotte's Reflections**: Speaking to companion at dinner, said: "My dear fellow, I don't think you've the gift of seeing very far. The truth is they don't know what to make of me;--and I don't intend that they shall. I'm playing my game, and there isn't one of 'em understands it except myself. It's no good my sitting here, you know. I shan't be able to move. How am I to get at you if I want anything?" **Many of Melmotte's staunchest supporters thought that he was very wrong not to show himself that day in the City. What good could he do pottering about among the chairs and benches in the banqueting room? In such a crisis, his work was in the City. Men will whisper forgery behind a man's back who would not dare even to think it before his face.**

## FORGERY RUMORS (Chapter 40 - NEW)
**The Rumor's Spread (Monday afternoon, Chapter 40)**: Horrid rumours prevailing in the City and spreading from the City westwards to the House of Commons, which was sitting with prospect of adjournment at seven o'clock due to Imperial banquet. Word "forgery" was whispered by more than one pair of lips. Nature of rumour not thoroughly understood by those who propagated it.

**Dolly Longestaffe as Parent of Rumor (Chapter 40 - CRITICAL)**: Dolly Longestaffe, with unhesitating resolution and nothing awed by his father, went to his attorney, Mr. Squercum, immediately after Friday when Mr. Longestaffe first took his seat at Railway Board. Dolly possessed fine qualities but veneration was not one of them. Told his father: "I don't know why Mr. Melmotte is to be different from anybody else. When I buy a thing and don't pay for it, it is because I haven't got the tin, and I suppose it's about the same with him. It's all right, no doubt, but I don't see why he should have got hold of the place till the money was paid down." Father warned: "You'll ruin me and yourself too, if you go to such a man as that. Why can't you trust Mr. Bideawhile? Slow and Bideawhile have been the family lawyers for a century." Dolly made remark as to old family advisers which was by no means pleasing to father's ears, and went his way. Father knew his boy would go to Squercum. He wrote timid letter to Mr. Melmotte, which had no result; and then, on the next Friday, again went into the City and encountered perturbation of spirit and sheer loss of time.

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty. Never owed shilling he couldn't pay. Firmly opposed Melmotte connection on principle. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless. Declared love to Henrietta anew; determination unshaken. Visited Ruby at Islington; warned her against Felix; extracted promise not to see him again. Encountered Paul and Mrs. Hurtle at Lowestoft; greeted coldly; reproved Paul severely. Counselled marriage with her would be destruction. Upon Paul's return, expressed satisfaction: "Let her follow you, and bear it. Of course you must suffer the effects of your own imprudence." **Chapter 39: Mr. Hepworth visited him one morning; they discussed attempted elopement. Roger said: "I know nothing about it, and I do not intend to ask." Hepworth opined Felix "A failure! Of course he's a failure, whether rich or poor;--a miserable imposition, a hollow vulgar fraud from beginning to end." Philosophical Discussion with Bishop: Roger discussed Melmotte's fitness for Parliament. Roger argued: "Men reconcile themselves to swindling. Then there comes the jealousy that others should be growing rich with the approval of all the world. It seems to me that the existence of a Melmotte is not compatible with a wholesome state of things in general." Bishop countered: existence of Melmotte not necessarily pernicious if he would vote Conservative; country is changing. Argued improvement proceeds from society as whole.** **Father Barham at Carbury Manor**: Roof blown off Father Barham's cottage by wind; Roger Carbury offered him shelter while damage being repaired. Shelter much more comfortable than priest's own establishment; Father Barham in clover.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway
**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City through New Mexico/Arizona into Mexico, terminating Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Stock at par; shares sold at premium. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not building railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury (attempted to flee), Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague. **Board meeting Chapter 39: Sir Felix did not attend; nor did Paul Montague. Lord Nidderdale had declined. After Board, Melmotte and Cohenlupe retired together.** Chapter 40: Melmotte and two Grendalls just come over from their work in the square; financier full of priest's visit.

## Lord Nidderdale and Marquis of Auld Reekie (Chapter 40)
**Nidderdale's Doubts and Determination**: That absurd elopement, which Melmotte declared really to mean nothing—romance of a girl who wanted one little fling before settling down—was perhaps his strongest objection. Sir Felix, no doubt, had not gone with her; but one doesn't wish to have one's intended wife even attempt to run off with anyone but oneself. **"She'll be sick of him by this time, I should say," his father said to him. "What does it matter, if the money's there?" Marquis seemed to think escapade had simply been the girl's revenge against his son for having made his arrangements so exclusively with Melmotte, instead of devoting himself to her. Nidderdale acknowledged to himself that he had been remiss. Told himself she was possessed of more spirit than he had thought. By the Sunday evening he had determined that he would try again. Expected plum would fall into his mouth. Would now stretch out his hand to pick it.** **The Affair's Abnormal Difficulties**: Perhaps Marquis had been wrong in flying at wealth reputed to be almost unlimited, but which was not absolutely fixed. Couple of hundred thousand pounds down might have been secured with greater ease. But here there was prospect of endless money—inheritance which might not improbably make Auld Reekie family conspicuous for its wealth even among most wealthy of nobility. Old man fallen into temptation; abnormal difficulties resulted. Latterly two difficulties culminated: young lady preferred another gentleman, and disagreeable stories were afloat, not only as to way in which money had been made, but even as to its very existence.

## Minor Characters
Didon (Marie's attendant, executed elopement plan). Miles Grendall (Secretary to Melmotte; does not pay debts of honour). Robert (Marie's servant; departed 6 A.M. Wednesday with big boxes). Lord Alfred Grendall (absolutely dependent on Melmotte; born and bred gentleman; found position under Melmotte almost insupportable; invested part of recent savings in cutting whip; paced back to Mount Street thinking of escape from servitude). Dolly Longestaffe (at club Monday evening; banished by hunger from Board meeting; parent of forgery rumor via attorney Squercum). Village characters: Aessa, Ellan Lindner, Manelle, Nylis Corrett. Harbor town scenes: Gulls, salt and tar smells, wind off water.
